This is a great question with direct practical importance for reading Quaker genealogical records. Here's the full history:

---

## Why Quakers Used Numbered Months

### The Core Religious Objection

When George Fox founded the Religious Society of Friends (Quakers) in England in the 1640s–50s, one of their core testimonies was **avoiding anything rooted in paganism or idolatry**. The standard month and day names were almost entirely derived from pagan deities:

| Name | Origin |
|---|---|
| January | *Janus*, Roman god of doorways |
| February | *Februa*, Roman purification rite |
| March | *Mars*, Roman god of war |
| April | possibly *Aphrodite*, or Latin *aperire* |
| May | *Maia*, Roman goddess |
| June | *Juno*, Roman goddess |
| July | *Julius* Caesar (deified) |
| August | *Augustus* Caesar (deified) |

(September–December are at least numerically honest — from Latin *septem*, *octo*, *novem*, *decem*, though misaligned after calendar reforms.)

The days of the week were equally pagan:

| Name | Origin |
|---|---|
| Sunday | the Sun |
| Monday | the Moon |
| Tuesday | *Tyr*, Norse god |
| Wednesday | *Woden/Odin*, Norse god |
| Thursday | *Thor*, Norse god |
| Friday | *Frigg/Freya*, Norse goddess |
| Saturday | *Saturn*, Roman god |

For Quakers, speaking or writing these names was tantamount to casually honoring false gods — a violation of their **testimony of integrity and simplicity**.

### Part of a Broader Plain Speech Tradition

Numbered months fit alongside other distinctively Quaker practices:
- Using *thee/thou* instead of *you* for one individual (resisting social class flattery)
- Refusing to remove hats before magistrates or kings
- Refusing to take oaths (a plain "yea" or "nay" was sufficient)
- Refusing to use honorific titles like *Lord* or *Sir*

It was a coherent, principled plainness applied consistently to language.

---

## The Critical Genealogical Complication: The Calendar Shift

This is where it gets tricky for researchers. England operated on the **Julian (Old Style) calendar** until the Calendar Act of 1750, which took effect **in September 1752**. Under the Old Style calendar:

- **The legal new year began March 25** (Lady Day), not January 1.
- So for Quakers following the civil year order, **First Month = March**.

| Quaker Month | Old Style (before 1752) | New Style (after 1752) |
|---|---|---|
| First Month | March | January |
| Second Month | April | February |
| Third Month | May | March |
| … | … | … |
| Tenth Month | December | October |
| Eleventh Month | January | November |
| Twelfth Month | February | December |

This means a Quaker record reading **"10th day, 1st mo, 1739"** actually means **March 10, 1739** — *not* January 10.

After 1752, Quakers gradually realigned so that First Month = January, but the transition was not instantaneous or uniform across meetings.

---

## Practical Tips for Reading Quaker Records

1. **Always check the year** — if it's before 1752, assume First Month = March and count forward.
2. **Watch for double-dating** — some Quakers wrote dates like "10th, 1 mo, 1739/40" to acknowledge the ambiguity around the January–March period.
3. **Monthly Meeting minutes** often use this system consistently; birth, marriage, and death registers do too.
4. **The convention persisted well into the 19th century** in some American meetings, even after the calendar reform made it unnecessary.

Quaker records are remarkably well-preserved and detailed — but misreading a numbered month can throw a birth date off by nearly a year, so this distinction is essential.

## What "15 February 1750/1" means

This is a **double-dated year** — a standard English clerical practice used when the civil (legal) year and the historical year disagreed.

### The background

In England before 1752, the **legal new year began on 25 March** (Lady Day), not 1 January. That meant the months of January, February, and most of March belonged to the *old* legal year, even though most educated people — and most of Europe — already counted a new year from 1 January.

To avoid ambiguity, careful clerks wrote **both years** for dates falling in that January–24 March gap:

| Part of the notation | What it means |
|---|---|
| **1750** | The Old Style (legal/civil) year — England's official year had not yet turned |
| **1751** | The New Style year — the historical/modern year already in progress since 1 January |

---

### What the tool resolved

| | Date |
|---|---|
| **As recorded (Old Style)** | 15 February 1750/1 |
| **Converted (New Style)** | 15 February **1751** |

*Rule applied: double-dated year resolved to the later (New Style) year.*

---

### Which year to use in your research notes

**Use 1751** — the New Style year — in your research notes, with a bracketed note to show you interpreted it:

> 15 February 1750/1 [**1751 NS**]

This is the standard genealogical convention. It lets future readers know the record itself shows the double date, while making clear which modern year you're filing the event under. If you record it as 1750, you'll be off by a year relative to every modern reference, and the marriage will appear to pre-date events that actually happened first.

In England before 1752, the **legal year began on 25 March** (Lady Day). Clerks writing dates between **1 January and 24 March** would often show *both* the Old Style year (the legal year still in progress) and the New Style year (the year that had already begun by common reckoning) — for example, "6 February 1750/1" means 1750 OS but 1751 NS.

---

## Why 25 March is the exception

**25 March is Lady Day itself — the exact day the Old Style year turns over.** On that date, the Old Style year and the New Style year are the same. There is no gap to bridge, so a double-date slash on 25 March is contradictory on its face. The tool declines to resolve it, because resolving it would be a guess.

1. **Do not automatically write 1751.** The slash doesn't mean the same thing here as it does on a January date.

3. **Note the anomaly in your research notes.** Record the date exactly as written — *25 March 1750/1* — and add a note explaining that the slash is atypical on Lady Day and that surrounding entries were checked to determine the intended year.

---

Record the date **as written**: `25 March 1750/1`. Until you've confirmed the clerk's intent from context, that is the most accurate representation. If surrounding entries confirm one year, you can record your interpretation alongside the original form — e.g., `25 March 1750/1 [interpreted as 25 March 1751 NS based on register context]`.
